description_full: Patrick Industries, Inc. manufactures and distributes component and materials for recreational vehicle, marine, powersports, manufactured housing, and industrial markets in the United States, Mexico, China, and Canada. The company operates through Manufacturing and Distribution segments. Its Manufacturing segment manufactures and sells laminated for furniture, shelving, wall, countertop, and cabinet products; cabinet doors, fiberglass bath fixtures, and tile systems; vinyl printing, amplifiers, tower speakers, soundbars, and subwoofers; solid surface, granite, and quartz countertop fabrication; aluminum products; fiberglass and plastic components; decorative vinyl and paper laminated panels; softwoods lumber; custom cabinetry; polymer-based and other flooring products; and dash panels. This segment also provides wrapped vinyl, paper, and hardwood profile mouldings; interior passage doors; air handling products; slide-out trim and fascia; treated, untreated, and laminated plywood; fiberglass and plastic helm systems and components; boat towers, tops, trailers, and frames; adhesives and sealants; thermoformed shower surrounds; specialty bath, and closet building products; wiring and wire harnesses; aluminum and plastic fuel tanks; CNC molds, composite parts, and marine hardware and accessories; slotwall panels and components; and other products. The company's Distribution segment distributes pre-finished wall and ceiling panels, drywall and finishing products, electronic and audio systems, appliances, and marine accessories; wiring, electrical, and plumbing products; fiber reinforced polyester products; and cement siding, raw and processed lumber, interior passage, roofing, laminate, and ceramic flooring, shower doors, furniture, fireplaces and surrounds, interior and exterior lighting products, and other products. This segment also offers transportation and logistics services. Patrick Industries, Inc. was incorporated in 1959 and is based in Elkhart, Indiana.

financial_summary: Patrick Industries, Inc. is a mid-cap consumer cyclical business with a $2.6B market cap on $4.0B of annual revenue.
The top line has compounded at -7% over the past three years and +16% annually across the full decade, and a shrinking top line is the hardest headwind any business can overcome.

Returns on capital run at 9% against a 9% cost of capital, which means the business barely earns its keep economically, and 18% gross margins are typical of commodity economics where competitors can replicate the product cheaply.

The business throws off $246M in free cash flow — roughly 6 cents on every revenue dollar, which is the owner-earnings figure that actually belongs to shareholders, and cash conversion sits at 2.44× so those profits are backed by real cash.
On the balance sheet, debt is moderate at 2.8× net debt/EBITDA, serviceable in normal conditions but worth watching through a downturn, and interest coverage of 16× is fortress-like.
Shareholder yield of 3.4% reflects a genuine commitment to returning capital rather than empire-building, and insiders hold 4.1% of the shares.

sector_headwinds.text: Very elevated short interest (23.7% of float) — sophisticated money is betting against the business
Revenue growth in the bottom decile of Consumer Cyclical peers — losing share inside the profit pool
Low reinvestment-driven growth suggests the compounding engine has stalled
Consumer demand is fundamentally cyclical — a recession compresses both unit volume and pricing power, and operating leverage cuts both ways.
E-commerce margin compression and tariff exposure — digital competition erodes pricing power while trade policy reshuffles supply-chain cost structures overnight.
Brand relevance decay — shifting consumer preferences and social-media-driven trends can strand inventory and invalidate positioning faster than product cycles can adapt.

sect: Its 7% operating margin is roughly in line with the Consumer Cyclical median (7%).
It earns less of the sector's profit than its revenue share would suggest (0.88x).
Over five years it has been losing share of the sector profit pool (-5.4% a year).
The sector is fragmented and competitive (HHI 0.03 across 377 companies in the universe; the top four hold 26% of revenue), so pricing power is hard to come by.
mkt: The shares are in a steep downtrend, down 35% over the past year excluding the latest month.
The price sits mid-way through its 52-week range, 46% below the high.
With annualised volatility of 39% and a beta of 1.06, it moves roughly with the market, though its beta has shifted (1y -0.02 vs 5y 1.08), so read it loosely.
About $41.0M trades a day, enough to build a position, and interest is running hot at 1.6x its yearly average volume.
In past sell-offs it fell 69% in the 2020 crash, 46% in the 2022 bear market and 97% in 2008.
val: The stock trades 28% below its DCF fair value of $112, a meaningful margin of safety.
The fair-value models disagree (dispersion 16%), and the Monte Carlo range runs $84.48 to $149 (P10-P90), so treat the estimate as noisy.
On multiples it looks cheap against Consumer Cyclical peers: P/FCF 10.5 vs 16.7 (sector median).
Against its own history it is dear: the EBIT multiple sits 19% above its 10-year median.
Earnings yields are mixed: an FCF yield of 9.5% (above the risk-free rate) and an EBIT/EV of 6.7% (vs the 8% bar).
The 12 covering analysts target $97.58 on average, 21% above the price.
prof: ROIC of 9% earns above the cost of capital of 8.5%, but the 1pp spread is short of the 7pp moat bar; returns have swung a lot from year to year (CV 0.38).
It runs a 18% gross margin and converts 6% of revenue into free cash flow.
Earnings quality looks solid: a Piotroski score of 8/9 and cash conversion of 2.44x.
ROE of 11% comes mostly from margins and asset turnover rather than leverage (2.6x equity multiplier).
It spends 0.5% of revenue on stock compensation.
hlth: Leverage is moderate at 2.8x net debt to EBITDA ($26.4M of cash against $1.3B of debt), above the 1.5x gate, with interest covered 16.3x.
No distress or manipulation flags (Altman Z 3.1, in the safe zone).
growth: Revenue has compounded at -6.8% over 3 years, 9.7% over 5 years and 15.7% over 10 years, so growth is decelerating.
Net reinvestment is nil (capex and working capital no more than cover depreciation), so fundamental growth is near zero.
Free cash flow has compounded 14.0% a year over five years.
Capex runs only 0.5x depreciation (2.1% of sales), so the asset base is being harvested rather than grown.
Its Rule of 40 score is 15, below the 40 that marks a healthy growth business.
It has beaten earnings estimates by 7.4% on average.
own: Insiders own a modest 4.1%, and reported institutional holdings exceed 100% of shares (a sign of heavy share lending).
Insider trading is two-way: 10 purchases and 2 sales over the past year, net $1.2M bought.
It returns 3.4% a year to shareholders (1.2% in buybacks and 2.3% in dividends).
The share count has shrunk 1.8% a year over five years, steadily raising each holder's stake.
Short interest is elevated at 23.7% of the float, 6.6 days to cover.
